Issued at 500 AM CDT Fri Sep 25 2026

An upper level ridge is tilting through the Northern Plains 
early this morning over weak surface flow between broad high 
pressure that stretches from Michigan through southern Quebec 
and low MSLP ahead of a potent upper level trough over the 
Pacific Northwest. Dense fog has already developed across much 
of central and eastern North Dakota and may continue to expand 
westward until an hour or two after sunrise. The fog should 
lift by late morning, but there is uncertainty in how long low 
clouds could linger. The RAP, which tends to handle low stratus 
better than other deterministic models, favors a mostly cloudy 
sky prevailing along and east of Highway 83 through the entire 
day. Highs this afternoon are expected to reach the 70s where 
sunshine is more prevalent (western ND) and 60s where clouds are
more prevalent (central and east). Model soundings to the south
and east of Bismarck show favorable conditions for drizzle this
morning. This may continue into the afternoon, but there will 
likely be a transition in drop-size distribution from drizzle 
to light rain showers. The showers will initially be isolated 
in the presence of only weak low level ascent, but a shortwave 
lifting north from the Central High Plains will increse chances 
for showers across the eastern half of the state this evening 
through tonight. Only light rain amounts are anticipated 
tonight, with ensembles favoring one to two tenths of an inch 
at most. Breezy conditions are expected today through tonight, 
with south-southeast winds around 15 to 20 mph. The breezy 
winds combined with extensive cloud cover will keep overnight 
low temperatures near record warm values in the mid to upper 
50s.

Light rain should depart to the east Saturday morning as the 
Pacific Northwest trough ejects into Alberta/Saskatchewan and 
becomes stacked over its occluding surface cyclone. The 
attendant cold front is forecast to enter western North Dakota 
Saturday morning, slowly progressing eastward and reaching 
central North Dakota by late afternoon/early evening. There is 
a low chance for light rain ahead of the front in northwest 
North Dakota Saturday morning, but measurable precipitation is 
unlikely. The front will carry a much drier air mass and gusty 
west-northwest winds into western North Dakota, but the earlier 
timing of strongest winds (midday) compared to the lowest RH 
(late afternoon) should keep fire weather conditions below even
near-critical levels. The warmest highs in the mid 70s on 
Saturday are likely to occur just ahead of the front due to 
compressional heating, with upper 60s and lower 70s expected 
elsewhere.

A cooler air mass will continue to filter into the region from 
the northwest on Sunday, but highs are still forecast to reach 
the mid 60s to lower 70s. By Sunday evening, shortwave energy 
ejecting from the base of a trough digging into northern 
California will begin approaching the Northern Plains. Lee 
cyclogenesis is forecast over Wyoming, eventually stretching 
into a positivly-tilted inverted trough on account of an 
approaching northern stream wave on Monday. Strong low level 
warm air advection/moisture transport ahead of the lead 
shortwave in an anomalously high precipitable water environment
is expected to result in widespread showers with embedded 
thunderstorms across much of the state Sunday evening into 
Monday morning. Increasing MUCAPE on the order of 1000 J/kg may
contribute to high rainfall rates, and there is a risk of 
training convection with forecast deep layer wind vectors 
perpendicular to low level moisture transport vectors. There 
may also be a conditional risk for strong to severe 
thunderstorms over this time period, but just a few hundred 
meters difference in elevated inflow layer could greatly 
regulate effective bulk shear, and point-specific model 
hodographs above 2 km are chaotic and generally not long. Due 
to the elevated nature of convection, the most likely hazard 
from a strong to severe storm through Monday morning would be 
large hail, for which low probabilities are highlighted by CSU 
machine learning guidance over southwest and south central 
North Dakota.

On Monday afternoon, the approaching northern stream wave under
a coupled jet streak could produce another round of showers and
thunderstorms that may or may not act as an extension of the 
first round. Afternoon thunderstorms would have a higher 
probability of being surface-based, but it is not a guarantee 
and would likely be limited to south central North Dakota along 
the inverted trough/cold front axis. A low CAPE/high shear 
environment could promote strong to severe storms Monday 
afternoon, with deep layer shear and wind vector orientation 
favoring a linear mode with damaging winds as the main hazard.
